# Annual Report 2025: Program Overview

---

## 1. Executive Summary

In 2025, Riverstone Shire Libraries delivered a total of 14 programs across our five branch locations and two outreach sites. This represents a modest but deliberate consolidation compared with previous years, reflecting our strategic decision to focus on depth and repeat engagement rather than one-off events. The annual report states that Riverstone Shire Libraries total_programs_run_2025 was 14 programs. Record status: current.

Attendance remained steady throughout the year, with school holiday periods and the winter reading challenge generating the strongest participation. The Community Programs Team continued to prioritise partnerships with local schools, aged-care facilities, and community groups, ensuring that our programming reached audiences beyond the library walls.

This report provides a complete listing of programs delivered, attendance data, and a summary of highlights and challenges encountered during the year.

---

## 2. Program Listings and Attendance Summary

The following table lists all programs delivered in 2025. Attendance figures are drawn from the Eventbrite registration system, in-branch sign-in sheets, and facilitator headcounts where registration was not used. Where a program ran multiple sessions, attendance is aggregated across all sessions.

**Total programs run: 14**

---

## 3. Attendance Overview

Total attendance across all programs for 2025 was **1,240** individual attendances. This figure includes repeat attendees across multiple sessions of the same program but does not include visitors who used library spaces without participating in programmed activities.

Attendance was distributed unevenly across the year, with peaks during:

- January (Summer Reading Club)
- July (The Great Winter Read)
- School holiday weeks in April and October (Storytime and Craft and Chat special sessions)

The quietest months were February and November, where school commitments and public holidays reduced participation in after-school and evening programs.

---

## 4. Program Highlights

### 4.1 Summer Reading Club

The Summer Reading Club ran across eight sessions in January and early February, with a total attendance of 214 children. The program included a mix of reading challenges, craft activities, and a finale event featuring a local children's author. Feedback from parents was overwhelmingly positive, with several families attending multiple sessions.

### 4.2 The Great Winter Read

Held throughout July, this reading challenge invited participants of all ages to track their reading over the month. The program attracted 156 registered participants, with 89 completing the challenge and receiving a certificate. The program saw strong participation from the 60+ age group, which was a notable shift from previous years.

### 4.3 Digital Literacy Basics

This six-session workshop series for seniors was developed in response to demand identified in 2024. Sessions covered topics including using email, online safety, accessing government services online, and using the library's e-resources. Attendance was strong (89 total), and several participants requested follow-up one-on-one appointments, which were accommodated through the Tech Help program.

---

## 5. Challenges and Learnings

- **Staffing capacity:** The Homework Help Hub and Storytime programs placed significant demands on staff time. Volunteer support for Homework Help was essential, but maintaining a consistent volunteer roster proved challenging during term breaks.
- **Weather disruptions:** Two Storytime sessions in March and one Craft and Chat session in November were cancelled due to severe weather warnings and power outages.
- **Venue constraints:** The Riverstone Central meeting room was at capacity for several Author Talk and Poetry Open Mic sessions. This limited our ability to accommodate walk-in attendees.
- **Promotional reach:** Programs targeting young adults (18–30) continued to see lower attendance than other demographics. Social media promotion improved in the second half of the year, but further work is needed.
### 5.3 Youth Programs

Youth programming (ages 12–18) continued to face engagement challenges, with attendance remaining lower than other demographics. The monthly Teen Gaming Night averaged 11 attendees per session, slightly below the 2024 average of 13. The Anime Club, introduced in August, attracted a small but consistent group of 8–10 regular attendees.

The school holiday Minecraft workshops were the exception, with strong demand. Three workshops were held in January and two in July, with total attendance of 64. These sessions filled within 48 hours of opening registration, and a waiting list of 23 names was recorded for the July workshops.

### 5.4 Adult Programs

Adult programming encompassed author talks, book clubs, craft sessions, and the Poetry Open Mic series. Author talks remained popular, with six sessions held across the year. The September talk featuring a prominent Australian crime fiction writer drew the largest audience of the adult programme, with 54 attendees.

The three library book clubs (Riverstone Central, Northgate, and Westfield) met monthly, with combined attendance of 312 across the year. The Craft and Chat group, held fortnightly, maintained steady attendance of approximately 10 participants per session, with one November session cancelled due to the power outage noted in Section 5.

The Poetry Open Mic series, held quarterly, saw growing interest. The November session attracted 38 attendees, the highest for the series, and several participants expressed interest in a monthly format for 2026.

According to the annual report, Riverstone Shire Libraries program_attendance_total_2025 was 1240 attendees. Record status: current.

### 5.5 Seniors Programs

Seniors programming expanded significantly in 2025, driven by the introduction of the Digital Literacy Basics series (Section 4.3) and continued demand for social connection programmes. The Seniors Morning Tea, held monthly, averaged 24 attendees per session, up from 18 in 2024.

The Digital Literacy Basics series ran twice during the year: a six-session series in March–April and a repeat series in September–October. Combined attendance was 89. The Tech Help one-on-one appointments, offered in response to demand from workshop participants, provided 47 individual sessions between May and November.

The library also hosted two one-off Seniors Information Days, covering topics such as aged care services and scam awareness. These events drew a combined attendance of 86.

### 5.6 Attendance Trends and Observations

Several trends emerged across the 2025 programme year:

- **Growth in children's holiday programmes:** Attendance at holiday programmes increased by 22% compared to 2024, with the April and October programmes particularly strong. This is attributed to the introduction of themed programmes and improved promotion through local schools.
- **Increased seniors participation:** Seniors attendance grew by 31%, reflecting both the expanded digital literacy offering and the popularity of the monthly morning teas. Several seniors attended multiple programme types, indicating cross-promotion between activities is effective.
- **Youth engagement remains a focus area:** Despite the success of the Minecraft workshops, regular youth programming continues to underperform relative to other demographics. Feedback from the Youth Advisory Group (established in August) suggests that timing and promotion are key barriers.
- **Venue capacity constraints:** The Riverstone Central meeting room reached capacity at 11 sessions during the year. This affected author talks and the Poetry Open Mic series in particular. Options for alternative venues are discussed in Section 7.
## 6. Financial and Resource Allocation

### 6.1 Budget Allocations by Programme Area

Table 6.1 outlines the budget allocations for the 2025 calendar year across the major programme areas, compared with the 2024 allocations. All figures are GST-exclusive.

| **Total** | **187,300** | **216,600** | **+29,300** | **+15.6%** |

The overall increase of $29,300 reflects the Council's commitment to expanding library programming, with the largest proportional increases directed toward Seniors Programmes and Adult Learning and Digital Literacy. These increases align with the attendance growth reported in Section 5 and with the strategic priorities outlined in the Library Strategic Plan 2023–2027.

### 6.2 Staffing and Hours

The budget allocation document states Riverstone Shire Libraries staff_hours_allocated_2025 was 1200 hours. Record status: current. This allocation, which remains current for the 2025/26 planning cycle, represents the total staff hours dedicated to programme delivery across all branches for the 2025 calendar year. The 1,200 hours were supplemented by 310 hours of casual staff time and 140 hours of volunteer assistance, bringing the total staffing resource for programme delivery to 1,650 hours. Volunteer hours were primarily concentrated in the Seniors Morning Tea series and the Digital Literacy Basics workshops, where trained volunteers provided one-on-one assistance to participants.

### 6.3 Resource Utilisation and Efficiency

The library achieved a programme attendance rate of 14.2 attendees per staff hour in 2025, up from 12.8 in 2024. This improvement was achieved despite the introduction of several new programmes that required additional planning time, reflecting increased efficiency in programme delivery and promotion.

The slight decline in attendance per session, from 51.2 to 47.6, is primarily attributable to the introduction of smaller, more targeted programmes such as the Tech Help one-on-one appointments and the smaller-format author talks held in the Northgate meeting room. These programmes were intentionally designed with lower capacity limits to provide a more intimate experience.

April Fools' Day – I was expecting a prank or two but nothing happened. Solid session, numbers were steady. 18 signed in, probably a couple more who didn't bother. The usual mix of regulars and new faces.

- Helped a man in his 60s set up two-factor authentication on his Gmail. He'd had an email account compromised last year and was nervous about it happening again. Walked him through the authenticator app on his phone, made sure he had backup codes written down somewhere safe. He seemed relieved.
- A mum came in with her teenage son – he needed to print a school assignment. She didn't have a USB and wasn't sure how to email the file from his phone. Got him logged into the public PC, showed him how to attach the file from his phone's email app. Printed it, and he was pretty happy. Mum said "this is so much easier than wrestling with our home printer."
- One woman asked if we could help with a scanned document – her landlord had sent her a lease renewal as a scan and she wanted to sign it without printing. I showed her how to use the free PDF editor on the public PCs. She signed it, saved it, emailed it back. Took about 15 minutes.

Session went well. 19 on the sheet, peak around 22. School holidays are starting soon so I expect numbers to dip a bit over the next couple of weeks.

I told him straight that it sounded like a mechanical failure and we don't have the gear to attempt a recovery in the library. He was disappointed but understood. I gave him the names of a couple of data recovery places in the city and warned him not to keep trying to plug it in, as that could make things worse. He took a photo of the info sheet I wrote out for him.
- A woman needed help with a Centrelink form online. The site kept timing out on her phone. Got her onto a public PC and she managed to get through it. She said she'd been trying for three days from home.

Small group tonight – only 9 signed in, but it was a really productive session. The rain kept a lot of people away, but those who braved it were in a good mood and stayed engaged the whole time.

We talked through the basics of router placement and how to name the network. He seemed to know a fair bit already, so it was more of a chat than a lesson. I gave him a few tips on securing the Wi-Fi with a strong password. He said he'd give it a go himself and come back if he got stuck.

Larger group again – 14 signed in. A few people brought friends along, which is always nice to see.

# Annual Report 2025: Program Overview

---

## 1. Executive Summary

In 2025, Riverstone Shire Libraries delivered a total of 14 programs across our five branch locations and two outreach sites. This represents a modest but deliberate consolidation compared with previous years, reflecting our strategic decision to focus on depth and repeat engagement rather than one-off events. The annual report states that Riverstone Shire Libraries total_programs_run_2025 was 14 programs. Record status: current.

Attendance remained steady throughout the year, with school holiday periods and the winter reading challenge generating the strongest participation. The Community Programs Team continued to prioritise partnerships with local schools, aged-care facilities, and community groups, ensuring that our programming reached audiences beyond the library walls.

This report provides a complete listing of programs delivered, attendance data, and a summary of highlights and challenges encountered during the year.

---

## 2. Program Listings and Attendance Summary

The following table lists all programs delivered in 2025. Attendance figures are drawn from the Eventbrite registration system, in-branch sign-in sheets, and facilitator headcounts where registration was not used. Where a program ran multiple sessions, attendance is aggregated across all sessions.

**Total programs run: 14**

---

## 3. Attendance Overview

Total attendance across all programs for 2025 was **1,240** individual attendances. This figure includes repeat attendees across multiple sessions of the same program but does not include visitors who used library spaces without participating in programmed activities.

Attendance was distributed unevenly across the year, with peaks during:

- January (Summer Reading Club)
- July (The Great Winter Read)
- School holiday weeks in April and October (Storytime and Craft and Chat special sessions)

The quietest months were February and November, where school commitments and public holidays reduced participation in after-school and evening programs.

---

## 4. Program Highlights

### 4.1 Summer Reading Club

The Summer Reading Club ran across eight sessions in January and early February, with a total attendance of 214 children. The program included a mix of reading challenges, craft activities, and a finale event featuring a local children's author. Feedback from parents was overwhelmingly positive, with several families attending multiple sessions.

### 4.2 The Great Winter Read

Held throughout July, this reading challenge invited participants of all ages to track their reading over the month. The program attracted 156 registered participants, with 89 completing the challenge and receiving a certificate. The program saw strong participation from the 60+ age group, which was a notable shift from previous years.

### 4.3 Digital Literacy Basics

This six-session workshop series for seniors was developed in response to demand identified in 2024. Sessions covered topics including using email, online safety, accessing government services online, and using the library's e-resources. Attendance was strong (89 total), and several participants requested follow-up one-on-one appointments, which were accommodated through the Tech Help program.

---

## 5. Challenges and Learnings

- **Staffing capacity:** The Homework Help Hub and Storytime programs placed significant demands on staff time. Volunteer support for Homework Help was essential, but maintaining a consistent volunteer roster proved challenging during term breaks.
- **Weather disruptions:** Two Storytime sessions in March and one Craft and Chat session in November were cancelled due to severe weather warnings and power outages.
- **Venue constraints:** The Riverstone Central meeting room was at capacity for several Author Talk and Poetry Open Mic sessions. This limited our ability to accommodate walk-in attendees.
- **Promotional reach:** Programs targeting young adults (18–30) continued to see lower attendance than other demographics. Social media promotion improved in the second half of the year, but further work is needed.

### 5.3 Youth Programs

Youth programming (ages 12–18) continued to face engagement challenges, with attendance remaining lower than other demographics. The monthly Teen Gaming Night averaged 11 attendees per session, slightly below the 2024 average of 13. The Anime Club, introduced in August, attracted a small but consistent group of 8–10 regular attendees.

The school holiday Minecraft workshops were the exception, with strong demand. Three workshops were held in January and two in July, with total attendance of 64. These sessions filled within 48 hours of opening registration, and a waiting list of 23 names was recorded for the July workshops.

### 5.4 Adult Programs

Adult programming encompassed author talks, book clubs, craft sessions, and the Poetry Open Mic series. Author talks remained popular, with six sessions held across the year. The September talk featuring a prominent Australian crime fiction writer drew the largest audience of the adult programme, with 54 attendees.

The three library book clubs (Riverstone Central, Northgate, and Westfield) met monthly, with combined attendance of 312 across the year. The Craft and Chat group, held fortnightly, maintained steady attendance of approximately 10 participants per session, with one November session cancelled due to the power outage noted in Section 5.

The Poetry Open Mic series, held quarterly, saw growing interest. The November session attracted 38 attendees, the highest for the series, and several participants expressed interest in a monthly format for 2026.

According to the annual report, Riverstone Shire Libraries program_attendance_total_2025 was 1240 attendees. Record status: current.

### 5.5 Seniors Programs

Seniors programming expanded significantly in 2025, driven by the introduction of the Digital Literacy Basics series (Section 4.3) and continued demand for social connection programmes. The Seniors Morning Tea, held monthly, averaged 24 attendees per session, up from 18 in 2024.

The Digital Literacy Basics series ran twice during the year: a six-session series in March–April and a repeat series in September–October. Combined attendance was 89. The Tech Help one-on-one appointments, offered in response to demand from workshop participants, provided 47 individual sessions between May and November.

The library also hosted two one-off Seniors Information Days, covering topics such as aged care services and scam awareness. These events drew a combined attendance of 86.

### 5.6 Attendance Trends and Observations

Several trends emerged across the 2025 programme year:

- **Growth in children's holiday programmes:** Attendance at holiday programmes increased by 22% compared to 2024, with the April and October programmes particularly strong. This is attributed to the introduction of themed programmes and improved promotion through local schools.
- **Increased seniors participation:** Seniors attendance grew by 31%, reflecting both the expanded digital literacy offering and the popularity of the monthly morning teas. Several seniors attended multiple programme types, indicating cross-promotion between activities is effective.
- **Youth engagement remains a focus area:** Despite the success of the Minecraft workshops, regular youth programming continues to underperform relative to other demographics. Feedback from the Youth Advisory Group (established in August) suggests that timing and promotion are key barriers.
- **Venue capacity constraints:** The Riverstone Central meeting room reached capacity at 11 sessions during the year. This affected author talks and the Poetry Open Mic series in particular. Options for alternative venues are discussed in Section 7.

### 6.2 Staffing and Hours

The budget allocation document states Riverstone Shire Libraries staff_hours_allocated_2025 was 1200 hours. Record status: current. ### 6.3 Resource Utilisation and Efficiency

The library achieved a programme attendance rate of 14.2 attendees per staff hour in 2025, up from 12.8 in 2024. This improvement was achieved despite the introduction of several new programmes that required additional planning time, reflecting increased efficiency in programme delivery and promotion.

Table 6.3 summarises key resource utilisation indicators for 2025.

| Indicator | 2024 | 2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total programme sessions | 312 | 358 | +46 |
| Total attendance | 15,980 | 17,040 | +1,060 |
| Attendance per session | 51.2 | 47.6 | −3.6 |
| Attendance per staff hour | 12.8 | 14.2 | +1.4 |
| Cost per attendee ($) | 11.72 | 12.71 | +0.99 |
| Cost per session ($) | 600.32 | 605.03 | +4.71 |
| Venue capacity reached (sessions) | 7 | 11 | +4 |

The slight decline in attendance per session, from 51.2 to 47.6, is primarily attributable to the introduction of smaller, more targeted programmes such as the Tech Help one-on-one appointments and the smaller-format author talks held in the Northgate meeting room. These programmes were intentionally designed with lower capacity limits to provide a more intimate experience.

**Section 7: What Would You Like to See Next Year? (continued)**

*Question: What one change would most improve the Summer Reading Challenge for next year? (Open text, single suggestion per respondent)*

Responses grouped by theme. Some comments appear in more than one theme where the suggestion covered multiple points.

**Theme: More prizes / better prize structure (n = 41)**
- "More prize tiers. Kids who read 10 books got the same as kids who read 30."
- "The prize draw was fine but it felt like a lottery. Maybe a guaranteed small prize for everyone who finishes?"
- "Better prizes for the older age group. My 12-year-old didn't care about the stickers."
- "Add a mid-challenge prize for reaching halfway. It kept us going last time but only for the little kids."
- "Prize for most improved reader or something like that. Not just most books."
- "The vouchers from the local shops were great. Could we get more of those?"
- "My daughter asked why the 14+ prizes were different from the younger ones. It seemed unfair to her."

**Theme: Longer challenge / more time (n = 18)**
- "Six weeks wasn't enough. We were away for two of them on holidays."
- "Start earlier in December so we can read over the whole summer, not just January."
- "Running it into February would help. School goes back but kids still want to read."
- "We found out about it in week two. A longer window would give families more time to join."

**Theme: Better app / online logging (n = 36)**
- "The app kept crashing on my phone. I went back to paper after the first week."
- "Make the app work offline. We don't always have reception at the beach."
- "The paper log was fine but the app should match it exactly. Ours didn't line up."
- "Let parents log for multiple children under one account. I had to switch profiles every time."
- "The scanning of book barcodes never worked for me. I typed the titles in manually."
- "Simpler login. I forgot my password every single week."
- "Add a reading timer in the app. My son wanted to see how many minutes he read, not just books."

**Theme: More book recommendations / reading lists (n = 29)**
- "The staff picks table was great. More of that, maybe grouped by age and interest."
- "A list of books that count for the challenge would help. We weren't sure what qualified."
- "Recommendations for reluctant readers. My son only wanted graphic novels and we weren't sure they counted."
- "More diversity in the suggested books. We struggled to find things outside the usual series."
- "A 'if you liked this, try this' list for each age group."
- "The library staff were brilliant at suggesting books, but we couldn't always get to the desk. A printed list would help."

**Theme: More activities / events (n = 22)**
- "Add a mid-challenge event like a book trivia night or a reading picnic in the park."
- "The author visit was the highlight. Could we have two next year?"
- "A weekly storytime tie-in was great. Maybe add a craft activity after."
- "Book club for the older kids. They wanted to talk about what they read."
- "A finish-line celebration party for everyone who completes. Even just a small one."

**Theme: Communication / reminders (n = 14)**
- "Email reminders weekly. We forgot to log half the books until the last week."
- "A text message when the challenge starts. We only saw the poster on the last day."
- "The phone call mid-challenge was lovely. More of that."
- "School newsletter mention. We don't visit the library every week in summer."

**Theme: Accessibility / inclusivity (n = 9)**
- "Large print books for the challenge. My grandmother read with my son but couldn't find large print titles on the list."
- "Include dyslexia-friendly books. My daughter has dyslexia and the font on some books was too hard."
- "A version of the log with pictures for pre-readers. My four-year-old wanted to join but couldn't mark his own books."

**Tuesday 18 March 2025 – Session 3 (4:00 pm – 6:00 pm)**

Session went well. Back to normal numbers after the quiet week. 17 on the sign-in sheet, but as usual a few latecomers didn't sign in. I'd say peak was around 20 in the room. The weather was nice which might have helped – people were out and about.

- Big one this week: a woman named Sandra came in with her laptop that had a virus. She'd clicked a link in an email that looked like it was from her bank. The laptop was running really slowly and she was worried about her banking details. I ran the free antivirus scan we have on the USB stick, found a few things, quarantined them. Told her to change her banking password from a different device. She was quite shaken – I sat with her for a while and talked through how to spot phishing emails. Gave her the printed guide we have.
- Two separate people asked about setting up video calls to family overseas. One was a grandmother wanting to call her grandson in England. She had an iPad but had never used FaceTime. Set it up with her and did a test call to my own phone. She was delighted – said she'd call her daughter tonight.
- One gentleman, aged about 70, wanted to know how to listen to audiobooks on his phone. He'd seen the library app advertised. I walked him through Libby and got him set up with his library card. He borrowed a pair of our headphones and sat in the corner listening for a bit.
- Also had a younger bloke, maybe mid-20s, needing help with his resume formatting. Not strictly tech support but we have the templates on the shared drive. Helped him get it into a PDF.

**Noted for next week:** The virus issue with Sandra – I should mention this to the team. We might want to do a small display or handout about phishing scams. Also, the Libby app was popular – might be worth checking how many people we've helped with it this year.

April Fools' Day – I was expecting a prank or two but nothing happened. Solid session, numbers were steady. 18 signed in, probably a couple more who didn't bother. The usual mix of regulars and new faces.

- Helped a man in his 60s set up two-factor authentication on his Gmail. He'd had an email account compromised last year and was nervous about it happening again. Walked him through the authenticator app on his phone, made sure he had backup codes written down somewhere safe. He seemed relieved.
- A mum came in with her teenage son – he needed to print a school assignment. She didn't have a USB and wasn't sure how to email the file from his phone. Got him logged into the public PC, showed him how to attach the file from his phone's email app. Printed it, and he was pretty happy. Mum said "this is so much easier than wrestling with our home printer."
- One woman asked if we could help with a scanned document – her landlord had sent her a lease renewal as a scan and she wanted to sign it without printing. I showed her how to use the free PDF editor on the public PCs. She signed it, saved it, emailed it back. Took about 15 minutes.
- Quiet one: a gentleman just wanted to use a computer to check his superannuation balance. He'd never used a mouse before, so it took a while. He was patient and left with a smile.

**Noted for next week:** The PDF signing thing came up twice now. Maybe worth adding it to the list of common tasks we mention in the intro spiel.

Showed him how to check the sender address and what to look out for. He said he'd been close to clicking it, so I was glad he brought it in.

**Noted for next week:** The scratch help took longer than expected. If that becomes a regular thing, we might want to set aside a dedicated table for coding help. Good energy tonight. 19 signed in, peak around 22. The weather was nice and a few kids came straight from sport. A couple of new faces again – seems like word is spreading.

- A boy in Year 6 wanted to make a stop-motion animation. He'd seen a video online and wanted to try it himself. Showed him how to set up a phone on a small tripod and take a series of photos. He made a short clip of a lego figure walking across the table. He was pretty chuffed with it.

**Facilitator Notes: Tech Tuesdays**

**12/08/25 – Session notes**

Full house tonight – 14 signed in, which is the most we've had for Tech Tuesdays since March. A few regulars brought friends along, which probably explains the jump. Good energy in the room, but also a bit noisy at times. Might be worth asking people to keep voices down near the back desks if it gets busy again.

- The Raspberry Pi boy (I really should learn his name, he's been coming for weeks now) finished the guessing game from last week and showed it to me. He'd added a scoring system on his own, which was great to see. We started a new project – a simple text-based adventure. We got as far as making a character move between rooms. He's picking up the logic faster than I expected. I've told him to have a think about what rooms he wants in his game before next week.
- The older gentleman from last week came back with his notebook full of notes. He'd been practising turning the tablet on and off and connecting to Wi-Fi at home. We did a video call setup – I used my own phone to call him so he could see how it works from the other end. He was really chuffed when he saw himself on screen. His daughter is in Perth, so we set up a test call to her that evening. It went through and she was thrilled. He's going to come back next week to do it again, just to build confidence.
- A woman in her fifties came in with a laptop that was running very slowly. She said it had been getting worse over the past month. We had a look at what was running in the background and found a lot of startup programs she didn't need. We disabled most of them and did a disk cleanup. She said it felt much snappier. I've noted her name and contact details in the box if she wants to come back for a follow-up.
- A younger guy, maybe early twenties, asked about setting up a home network. He'd just moved into a new place and wanted to connect a printer and a smart TV. We talked through the basics of router placement and how to name the network. He seemed to know a fair bit already, so it was more of a chat than a lesson. I gave him a few tips on securing the Wi-Fi with a strong password. He said he'd give it a go himself and come back if he got stuck.

**Noted for next week:** Bring a spare HDMI cable – someone asked about connecting a laptop to a TV and we didn't have one on hand. Also, the reading glasses suggestion from last week was a good one. Several people this week mentioned struggling with small text on screens. I'll see if we can get a pair or two from the front desk.

---

**19/08/25 – Session notes**

Smaller group this week – 7 signed in. School holidays are over, so that might be part of it. The weather was nice too, which never helps. Still, the people who came were keen and we got through a lot.

- The Raspberry Pi boy wasn't here this week. I hope he's okay – he's been pretty consistent. I'll keep the adventure game project aside for him.
- The older gentleman came back for his second video call practice. He'd written down the steps from last week and followed them himself this time. I only had to help with one small thing – he couldn't remember how to end the call. We went over it a couple of times and he wrote it down again. He said he'd practised with his sister over the weekend, so he's getting there.
- A new attendee, a woman in her sixties, brought in a laptop that wouldn't connect to her home Wi-Fi. We checked the basics – Wi-Fi was on, password was correct, but it still wouldn't connect. After a bit of digging, we found the network adapter was disabled in Device Manager. We enabled it and it connected straight away. She was relieved – she'd been about to buy a new laptop. I showed her how to check that setting herself if it ever happens again.
- A teenager came in with a phone that kept running out of storage. We went through her apps and cleared the cache on a few big ones. We also moved her photos to Google Photos and set up automatic backup. She said she'd been deleting apps to make space, so it was good to show her there was a better way.

**26/08/25 – Session notes**

Back up to 12 signed in this week. Good mix of regulars and a few new faces. The school-holiday lull seems to be over.

- The Raspberry Pi boy is back. He'd been away because his family went on holiday, not because anything was wrong – good to hear. We picked up where we left off on the adventure game. He'd been reading about Python loops while he was away, which surprised me. He said, "I just wanted to know how to make the door open more than once." We spent a good chunk of the session on that. He's picking it up faster than I expected.
- The older gentleman came in for his third video call practice. This time he wanted to call his daughter in Perth. We set it up and he managed the whole call himself – I just watched. He was chuffed. He said his sister had been helping him practise and he felt ready. I told him he didn't need to book a session every week if he didn't want to, but he said he'd still come in for the company. That's fine by me.
- A woman in her forties brought in an old desktop computer. She'd found it in her mum's garage and wanted to see if it could be used for email and photos. It was slow to start, but we got it going. We installed a lightweight browser and set up her email. The machine is old but it should cope with the basics. She said she'd bring it back if she had any trouble.
- New attendee, a man in his seventies, had a question about online banking. He was worried about scams. We talked through some basics – checking the URL, not clicking links in emails, using the bank's app instead of a browser. He took notes. He said he'd had a call last week from someone claiming to be from his bank, and he'd hung up, which was the right thing to do. I gave him the library's scam-awareness flyer and suggested he come to the internet safety session next month if he wanted more detail.

**Noted for next week:** The HDMI cable suggestion from last week came in handy – someone asked about it and we had one ready. We'll keep it in the tech kit. Also, the reading glasses are still getting used. I'll ask the front desk if we can get a second pair.

---

**02/09/25 – Session notes**

Quiet session – 6 signed in. It was a warm day and a few regulars texted to say they couldn't make it. No trouble, just a small group.

- The Raspberry Pi boy was here again. We got the door-opening loop working and he was pleased. He asked if we could make the game save his progress, so we started talking about files and storage. We didn't finish, but he's got a clear idea of what he wants to do. I'll help him with it next week.
- A woman came in with a tablet. She'd been given it by her son and couldn't get the keyboard to connect. It turned out the keyboard needed pairing in the Bluetooth settings – it had never been paired. We did that in a couple of minutes. She said she'd been trying to type on the screen and it was driving her mad. She was happy to have it sorted.
- The rest of the session was drop-in help. One person wanted to know how to back up photos from her phone to a USB stick. We did that. Another asked about printing from a phone – we showed them how to use the library's mobile printing service.

**Noted for next week:** The second pair of reading glasses arrived from the front desk – they're in the tech kit now. Also, I should print out a simple one-page guide on Bluetooth pairing. It came up twice this week and it's a common enough problem that a handout would help.

---

**09/09/25 – Session notes**

Larger group again – 14 signed in. A few people brought friends along, which is always nice to see.

**Noted for next week:** The Bluetooth handout went well – I gave out all the copies I'd printed. I'll print a few more. Also, someone asked about a workshop on phone photography. I'll mention it to Mia – she might be able to run one.
